hints: Think about the last piece of the best cutting. It is a mirror s[l..r] ending at the end of the string — and whatever is before it must itself be cut optimally.
1D DP: cut[i] = fewest cuts for the prefix of length i. To find all mirror pieces fast, expand around every centre (odd and even) instead of checking each substring separately.

1. Set cut[i] = i - 1 (worst case: every letter alone), with cut[0] = -1.
  2. For each centre c, expand l and r outward (both odd (c,c) and even (c,c+1)) while s[l] == s[r].
  3. Each time s[l..r] is a mirror, update cut[r+1] = min(cut[r+1], cut[l] + 1).
  4. Return cut[n].

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every way to cut the string (2<sup>n-1</sup> options) and check that each piece is a mirror.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Precompute an n×n table isPal[l][r], then cut[r] = min(cut[l-1] + 1) over mirror pieces.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Expand around centres while updating the cut array directly — no n×n table needed.

explain: For "noonabc": expanding around the centre between the two os finds "noon", so cut[4] = cut[0] + 1 = 0 (no cut needed for the first four letters). After that only single letters are mirrors, so each of a, b, c adds one cut: 3 in total. The cut[0] = -1 trick makes a piece starting at index 0 cost 0 cuts. Whole-string mirrors like "madam" return 0.
recognize: 'Cut into pieces that are each palindromes, fewest cuts' → prefix DP where the last piece is a palindrome, found by expanding around centres.
